title: Variational quantum eigensolver with linear depth problem-inspired ansatz for solving portfolio optimization in finance
abstract_summary: The authors propose two hardware-efficient, problem-inspired variational ansätze (CCC and CC) that prepare arbitrary Dicke states with linear nearest-neighbor CNOT depth and reduced parameter counts, tailored for binary portfolio optimization using a hard-constraint encoding and CVaR cost. They introduce a hybrid distributed computing (HDC) workflow combining circuit cutting, simultaneous sampling, measurement-error mitigation and fragment reuse, and demonstrate experiments on a superconducting device up to 55 qubits, reporting improved trainability and practical performance for NISQ-era financial optimization.
methodology_description: The authors design and evaluate a NISQ-oriented variational approach for binary integer portfolio optimization by constructing two problem-inspired, hardware-efficient variational ansatze (denoted CCC and CC) that prepare parameterized Dicke-state subspaces. The methodology replaces a soft-constraint QUBO penalty approach with a hard-constraint ansatz that enforces the budget (fixed Hamming weight k) in the state-preparation circuit. Each ansatz uses a single-layer staircase Un (built from local controlled-Ry and CNOT blocks optimized to minimal two-qubit gates) giving linear two-qubit gate depth and limited parameters. Optimization follows a VQE workflow that uses the CVaR objective (local cost) with various confidence levels α to improve trainability. To scale beyond single-device width limits they propose a hybrid distributed computing (HDC) scheme: classically partition the ansatz into subcircuits (columns/subspaces), apply circuit cutting (or qubit reuse) to create small fragments, perform simultaneous sampling of fragments, apply a problem-specific measurement-error mitigation exploiting Hamming-weight symmetry, and reuse fragments across parameter updates to reduce hardware submissions. They evaluate the approach with noise-free numerical simulation (pyQPanda) and superconducting quantum hardware experiments (up to 55 qubits for k=3 and a 12-qubit |D12_6> instance), compare CCC/CC ansatze to a hardware-efficient (HE) ansatz baseline, and use classical optimizers (COBYLA and SLSQP) with iterative CVaR-α schedules.
experimental_setup: Numerical simulations used pyQPanda; classical optimizers COBYLA (primary) and SLSQP (in fragment-reuse experiments). Hardware experiments run on a superconducting quantum processor (55-qubit device; 6-qubit sub-topology used in some runs). Ansatze use linear-nearest-neighbor connectivity and single-layer Un staircase circuits (CCC and CC variants). CVaR objective with confidence levels α ∈ {1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1} was used; maximum classical VQE iterations up to 500. Circuit cutting produced small fragments (e.g., 2–6 qubits) sampled N times per fragment (N chosen to satisfy Hoeffding bounds; example shot counts listed for initial experiments: 8000, 4000, 2000, 2000, 1000, 1000, 3000 across different configurations). Measurement-error mitigation exploited Hamming-weight symmetry and used assignment-matrix inversion (pmig = M^{-1} pnoisy) with renormalization.
dataset_used: Synthetic/market asset data generated via qiskit_finance.data_providers. Asset pools of varying sizes (simulations up to n=20 assets; hardware experiments used pools up to n=55 assets in k=3 case and n=12 for the |D12_6> case). Random seeds reported (e.g., seed=1000 for primary asset pools; seed=1213 used for a complementary test).

experiment_input.sizes: Simulations: n in [4,20] (examples up to 20); Hardware: up to n=55 for k=3 test, n=12 for |D12_6> test
experiment_input.preprocessing: Mean-variance portfolio model translated to binary integer selection x (xi in {0,1}); hard budget constraint implemented by restricting ansatz to fixed Hamming-weight (Dicke-state) subspace. For mapping to spin/qubit Hamiltonian, standard zi=1-2xi mapping referenced for soft-constraint comparison, but the implemented method encodes constraint into state-preparation circuit instead of a penalty term.

pipeline_steps: Design CCC and CC variational ansatze based on a single-layer staircase Un (3C and 2C building blocks respectively), optimized to minimal CNOT counts for LNN connectivity.
Map the portfolio optimization to a cost Hamiltonian for the fixed-budget subspace and adopt CVaR as the objective (minimize expectation over worst α-fraction).
For simulations: run VQE with COBYLA (default) across multiple random asset pools and parameter initializations; evaluate metrics (probability of optimal/feasible solution, run time).
For larger instances/hardware: partition the ansatz classically into subcircuits (one or more columns per subcircuit), cut or reuse qubits to produce small fragments.
Simultaneously sample all fragments (N shots each), then reconstruct full-bitstrings via sequential classical stitching (based on measured cut-qubit outcomes).

Apply problem-specific measurement-error mitigation leveraging Hamming-weight symmetry: set assignment matrix M accordingly, compute pmig = M^{-1} pnoisy, renormalize probabilities restricted to correct Hamming weight.
Use fragment-reuse: when parameters change only in certain fragments, reuse previously sampled fragments to reduce hardware submissions; update only affected fragments.

Optimize parameters classically with COBYLA (or SLSQP for certain fragment-reuse experiments), adapting CVaR confidence α (start smaller, anneal to 1.0) and iterate until convergence or maximum iterations (e.g., 500).

results_summary: The paper proposes two compact, problem-inspired, hardware-efficient variational ansatze (CCC and CC) that prepare Dicke-like subspaces with linear-nearest-neighbour-friendly, staircase circuit structure and analytically low two-qubit depth and parameter counts. They combine these ansatze with a hybrid distributed computing scheme (circuit cutting, simultaneous fragment sampling, a problem-specific measurement-error mitigation exploiting Hamming-weight constraints, and fragment reuse) to run portfolio-optimization experiments (CVaR objective) on a superconducting quantum processor. Numerical simulations and hardware runs (including experiments up to 55 qubits for k=3 and a 12-qubit balanced case) indicate improved trainability and higher probabilities of finding feasible/optimal solutions relative to a tested shallow hardware-efficient ansatz. The paper presents theoretical arguments that their partitioning approach reduces certain circuit-cut sampling overheads and advocates using restricted-expressibility ansatze plus local CVaR objectives for NISQ combinatorial problems.
performance_claims: [speculative] The CCC ansatz worst-case two-qubit (CNOT) depth scales linearly with n with a constant factor ≤ 2 (claimed in text and complexity analysis).
[speculative] Parameter counts: CCC uses ≈ nk − 3k^2/2 parameters; CC uses ≈ n(k+1)/2 − k^2/4 parameters (analytical expressions given in paper).

[supported] Experimental demonstration: portfolio optimisation experiments were executed on superconducting hardware with up to 55 qubits for |D_n^3⟩ instances and a 12-qubit |D_12^6⟩ instance (reported and plotted results).

[supported] For the benchmark |D8_2⟩ example the paper lists CNOT counts across several methods as [44, 27, 31, 22, 25] and reports their ansatz achieves the minimum CNOT count under LNN (22 CNOTs in that comparison).
[supported] Sampling complexity per subcircuit for evaluating CVaR_α is O(1/(α ε^2)) in their scheme (empirically used and argued in experiments/simulations).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors claim the HDC scheme and compact ansatze 'show great potential' to achieve quantum advantage for some NISQ-era portfolio tasks, but they do not demonstrate a provable or experimentally validated quantum advantage over classical methods; results are limited to improved performance versus a tested HE ansatz and resource comparisons, so any advantage remains speculative.
limitations: Restricted expressibility of the proposed CCC and CC ansatze (trade-off: fewer parameters / shallower circuits versus a smaller reachable state space).
CC ansatz produces non-target basis states for intermediate budgets (k in [3, n-3]) which require mitigation (e.g., symmetric partitioning) and can reduce efficiency.
Performance depends sensitively on asset ordering and parameter initialization (ordering and initialization can materially affect probability of finding optimal/feasible solutions).
Empirical demonstrations are limited in scale: experiments reported up to 55 qubits only for |D_n^3⟩ and up to 12 qubits for balanced |D_n^{n/2}⟩, so large-scale practicality remains unproven.
Method relies on small CVaR confidence level α for good performance; achieving target performance may require reducing α (more aggressive tail-focused objective) which affects sampling.

Hybrid distributed computing (HDC) sampling complexity reduction hinges on single-qubit cuts and the symmetry properties of Dicke-like states; the same reduction is not generally available for arbitrary circuits.
The HDC approach requires classically choosing and partitioning appropriate columns/subspaces; selecting these columns can be cumbersome and depends on asset correlations and problem structure.
Fragment reuse and some partitioning choices introduce bias (authors acknowledge introduced bias when reusing fragments), which may affect solution quality.
Experiments used only simple measurement-error mitigation; overall results remain constrained by hardware noise and limited/no advanced error mitigation applied.
[inferred] The circuit-cutting advantage (reduced sampling complexity) degrades or may not apply when multi-qubit cuts are necessary or when target states lack the required symmetry.

[inferred] The approach may not scale efficiently to large budgets k and large n without substantial additional techniques, because number of independent columns / subspaces grows and overlap management becomes challenging.

[inferred] The techniques assume availability of linear-nearest-neighbor connectivity and low-depth CNOTs; their advantages may diminish on hardware with different constraints or higher two-qubit error rates.

[inferred] The overall pipeline (many small fragments, classical postprocessing, and sequential reconstruction) may be limited by classical overheads (storage, stitching, and sampling orchestration) as scale increases.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Hybrid distributed computing (HDC) combining classical circuit cutting, simultaneous fragment sampling, measurement-error mitigation and fragment reuse enables experiments beyond device width (demonstrated up to 55 qubits) by reconstructing full bitstrings from small fragments.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Two problem-inspired variational ansatze (CCC and CC) prepare fixed-Hamming-weight Dicke subspaces with linear nearest-neighbour CNOT depth and reduced parameter counts, improving trainability for NISQ hardware compared to a generic hardware-efficient ansatz.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Empirical simulator and superconducting-hardware results report that CCC/CC outperform a hardware-efficient (HE) baseline in probability of sampling optimal/feasible solutions and in runtime for tested instances, supporting practical NISQ-era gains on small-to-moderate portfolio problems.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Enforcing hard constraints via state-preparation (fixed budget/Dicke encoding) instead of soft-constraint QUBO penalties yields better optimization landscapes and removes penalty-weight tuning.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Using CVaR as the local cost with annealed confidence levels (alpha schedule) and single-layer Un circuits aids convergence and empirical trainability, helping mitigate barren-plateau-like issues in practice.

#limitation:noise — Hardware noise impacts results and requires problem-specific measurement-error mitigation (Hamming-weight symmetry and assignment-matrix inversion); residual noise and mitigation limits affect empirical performance.

#limitation:qubit-count — Scaling to larger portfolio sizes depends on circuit cutting and fragment reuse; while demonstrated, this incurs classical overhead and sampling costs and may limit practical scalability for larger k or deeper circuits.
